- What I am
  - I’m a very large software program that generates text. I don’t “know” things the way people do, and I don’t have feelings or desires. I’m designed to predict what words come next in a sentence, based on patterns I learned from lots of text.

- How it works at a high level
  - Training: I was exposed to a huge amount of written material (books, articles, websites, etc.). During training, I learned which words tend to follow which other words in many different contexts.
  - Turning your words into something I can work with: When you type, your words are broken into small units (tokens), which I convert into numbers that the model can process.
  - Making a reply: I look at your words and the recent conversation, then predict the most likely next words step by step to build a complete answer. I do this using a network with many layers that “attends” to different parts of what you wrote to stay relevant.
  - Keeping context: I try to remember the recent parts of our chat so my reply fits with what we’ve talked about. I don’t have long-term memory between different chats unless a system is set up to store them.

- Do I understand what you’re saying?
  - Not in the way a person does. I don’t have beliefs, intentions, or awareness.
  - I simulate understanding by using patterns that have worked well in lots of text. That can make my responses feel thoughtful, but it’s still just pattern-matching and predicting.
  - I can be wrong or miss nuances, especially with tricky or new topics. If something seems off, you can ask me to explain differently or check with another source.

- Why this feels conversational
  - Because I’ve been trained on lots of human writing that’s meant to be read aloud or talked about. I try to respond in clear, natural language and to stay on topic from the conversation history.

- Important limits and tips
  - I don’t automatically pull in fresh information from the web unless a tool within the chat is used for that. My knowledge has a cutoff (things after that may be incomplete or uncertain).
  - I can introduce biases or plausible-sounding but incorrect details. If you’re ever unsure, it’s good to double-check.
  - Privacy: I only know what you share in this chat unless the system stores more, which you can usually control.

- A concrete analogy for your background

Here’s a simple, practical shakshuka method you can try with a basic skillet. I’ll note approximate times so you can gauge doneness without a thermometer.

Shakshuka – simple, practical version
- Ingredients (rough guide for 2 servings)
  - 1–2 tablespoons olive oil
  - 1 small onion, chopped
  - 1 bell pepper (any color), chopped
  - 2–3 cloves garlic, minced
  - 1 teaspoon ground cumin, 1 teaspoon paprika, pinch chili flakes (optional)
  - 1 can (14–15 oz) crushed or diced tomatoes (or use fresh tomatoes if you have them)
  - Salt and black pepper
  - 2–4 eggs
  - Fresh parsley or cilantro for garnish (optional)
  - Bread to serve (optional)

- Steps
  1) Sauté vegetables: Heat the oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and pepper and cook until soft, about 6–8 minutes.
  2) Bloom the spices: Add the garlic and spices. Cook about 1 minute until fragrant.
  3) Build the sauce: Add the tomatoes, a pinch of salt, and pepper. Simmer gently until the sauce thickens a bit, about 10–12 minutes. Taste and adjust seasoning.
  4) Make wells: Use a spoon to push the sauce toward the edges and create 2–4 shallow wells in the sauce.
  5) Add the eggs: Crack an egg into each well.
  6) Cook the eggs: Lower the heat, cover the pan, and cook until the whites set to your liking and the yolks are as runny or set as you prefer.
     - For runny yolks: about 6–8 minutes total from adding the eggs.
     - For a bit firmer yolks: 8–10 minutes.
     - For fully set yolks: 10–12 minutes or a touch longer.
  7) Finish and serve: Remove from heat. Garnish with parsley or cilantro if you have it. Serve with bread to scoop up the sauce and eggs.

Tips and tweaks
- If the sauce seems too thick, splash in a little water or broth to loosen it a bit.
- If you don’t have cumin or paprika, you can skip them and use a pinch of dried oregano or just garlic and salt for a milder version.
- If you prefer, you can finish the eggs in the oven after you add them to the wells: bake at 375°F (190°C) for about 6–8 minutes for a more uniform cook.
- Eggs in purgatory vibe: it’s quite similar—Italian-style tomato sauce with garlic and chili, and eggs gently poached in it. The main differences are usually the spice profile (fewer cumin/paprika, more oregano/basil) and sometimes a splash of olive oil or a bit of cheese stirred in at the end.
